quote: More importantly, I realized that I had always known this—that the real memory had always been lurking in a corner of my mind
content: This is a memory, recalled at fifteen, of an event at six or seven, reinterpreted, and then recounted years later as the origin of a discipline, and the reconstructive-memory literature says every layer of it is suspect. Memories of early childhood are sparse and heavily rebuilt at each retrieval; the felt certainty that one "always knew" a later interpretation is the knew-it-all-along effect, in which people misremember their earlier state of mind as containing what they know now (Fischhoff 1975). The essay reports the discovery of a suppressed truth; what the evidence permits is that a fifteen-year-old constructed a less flattering story and experienced the construction as recovery, which is what the construction of any vivid memory feels like. The sequence's founding moment, as told, is a case study in the phenomena Book I catalogued under hindsight and imagination inflation.

quote: Now I’m going to notice every time I do that, and clean out all my corners!
content: The discipline presumes access to the thing it is meant to catch. Motivated forgetting and suppression, to the extent they occur, work by keeping the unwanted content out of awareness; the think/no-think paradigm finds that people can make items harder to recall by practicing not thinking about them (Anderson & Green 2001), and the mechanism does not announce itself. A person who succeeds in shoving an unwanted truth into a corner does not, by construction, have a feeling of having done so to generalize over; the feeling the fifteen-year-old caught was the feeling of recovery, which is available, not the feeling of suppression, which is not. "Confirmation bias" is also the wrong label for what is described: the review literature reserves it for biased search and interpretation of evidence (Nickerson 1998), and the essay's phenomenon is closer to self-serving memory, for which introspective vigilance has no demonstrated effect.
